source.title: Tracing the Dynamics of Refusal: Exploiting Latent Refusal Trajectories for Robust Jailbreak Detection
source.authors: Xu-Lin Hu; Che Wang; Wei Yang Bryan Lim; Jian-Bo Gao; Zhongzi Chen

record.tranche_reason: The study builds a jailbreak detector using refusal-related hidden-state patterns and compares static RepE-style direction readouts as detectors. It does not test whether ablating or adding the claimed difference-in-means direction changes refusal behavior.
record.gate_note: The paper reports causal activation-patching results and detector results from static difference-in-means projections. The patching experiments manipulate localized hidden states, not the claimed direction; the RepE baselines measure detection performance, not refusal behavior. Those outcomes are recorded as related findings under none, not as tests of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study builds a jailbreak detector (SALO). Its causal tracing patches whole hidden states at layer-token positions rather than a difference-in-means direction. It never ablates or adds the Arditi direction, never edits weights, and never measures refusal rates under direction interventions. Its static diff-in-means readouts (Appendix D) are detection baselines scored by AUROC and DSR, not refusal behaviour. The claim that attacks suppress the terminal refusal direction is stated as a hypothesis and checked only through detector performance. The authors state they do not claim static directions are invalid for steering.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors conclude refusal is driven by sparse upstream layer-token anchors, with attenuated terminal signals, and that SALO exploits this to detect jailbreaks. They say static directions remain valid for steering but terminal or averaged readouts are insufficient for robust detection.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses causal activation patching and ROI-level class-contrast projections for analysis and detection; it does not apply the original single-direction ablation/addition recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Causal-refusal results vary with layer-window and token-window size; at TW=1 and TW=3 refusal-onset patches outperform final-token patches, while at TW=6 the final-token window slightly surpasses onset because it overlaps upstream positions. Detector performance is also evaluated under different ROI windows.

fits_no_version.finding: Patching full hidden states from harmful into benign minimal pairs induces refusal most strongly at tokens just after the harmful anchor in intermediate layers. The effect is weaker at the final token (Llama-3.2-3B: >0.6 vs ~0.3 at LW=3, TW=1) and grows with window size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal can be causally induced by patching localized upstream layer-token states; terminal-position patches are weaker unless the window overlaps upstream positions.

fits_no_version.finding: A terminal-token class-contrast (diff-in-means) readout flags almost no GCG prompts (0.38% Llama, 0.0% Qwen) at an XSTest 10%-FPR threshold. A mean-pooled readout flags all attacks but has near-chance XSTest AUROC (~48).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Static diff-in-means projections at the terminal token lose their harmful/benign separation under GCG suffixes. This is consistent with, but not a direct test of, attacks suppressing the refusal direction.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The causal tracing evidence is described as sufficiency-style evidence and does not identify necessary low-level circuit components. Several causal-tracing outcomes are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The authors also note limited evidence for ROI transfer to substantially larger models and that SALO depends on the model recognizing harmful intent.
record.rows_left_out: SALO detector scores, its ROI-sensitivity tables, and adaptive-attack detection results were omitted because they measure detector performance rather than the refusal-direction intervention or refusal behavior in the claim. The paper's claims about adaptive attacks and semantic collapse are likewise not direct tests of whether attacks suppress the claimed direction.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of a difference-in-means direction; no refusal or capability measurement under direction intervention.
No measurement of the refusal direction's projection under attacks. No training against ablation. The suppression claim is a hypothesis supported only by detector results.
The patching localizes positions, not directions; no affine, cone or multi-direction test.
Cites Zhao et al. 2025a but does not test the harm/refusal separation.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer.

record.verdict_notes: Arditi et al. is cited as background. The statement that GCG suppresses the refusal direction at the final token is an untested hypothesis, inferred indirectly from detector success. Direct-prompt detection rates for the RePE-Terminal readout are also low (13.27%, 50.38%), so the GCG drop is confounded by threshold calibration. It should not be read as evidence for V3.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not ablate or add the single difference-in-means direction, or measure its effect on refusal and general capability.
No weight edit or abliteration of released models is evaluated.
The study does not directly measure whether attacks suppress the claimed direction or train models against its ablation.
The study analyzes localized activation patterns, but does not test affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
The paper cites work on separate harmfulness and refusal representations but does not test that distinction.
No transfer of the claimed direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages is tested.
The study does not vary refusal-training procedures or stages.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Patched cached activations from a harmful prompt into a benign prompt at layer-token positions using a 3-layer sliding window; measured refusal induction.

conditions.value: minimal harmful-benign pair; example contrasts bomb and cake

rows.measure: Refusal Loss and successful full-refusal induction
rows.value: Figure shows localized positions with successful refusal induction and other positions with no or partial effect; no numerical values stated in text.
rows.note: The paper explains that low refusal-prefix loss without a star can reflect only a shared prefix, not a complete refusal. This patches localized activations, not a difference-in-means direction.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Aggregated causal-tracing patches over 40 malicious-benign prompt pairs, aligned relative to the semantic anchor.
rows.value: The text reports a concentrated peak at the tokens immediately after the semantic anchor in intermediate layers, followed by attenuation; the terminal position has a resurgence but remains below the earlier peak.
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative pattern; numerical rates are shown only in the figure.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Patched activation windows centered on the refusal-onset token.
rows.baseline: Final-token intervention under the same window configuration
rows.note: Text says this onset result exceeds the final-token result, which remains near 0.3.
rows.check: Conditions should note the Appendix B experiments use N=160 adversarial-benign pairs. The value is approximate and read from text.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Patched activation windows centered on the final token.
rows.baseline: Refusal-onset intervention under the same window configuration
rows.note: The text contrasts this with an onset peak of approximately > 0.6.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared activation patching at refusal-onset and final-token regions.
rows.baseline: Final-token intervention compared with refusal-onset intervention
rows.value: At TW=1 and TW=3, the refusal-onset intervention significantly outperforms the final-token intervention; numerical values are figure only.
rows.note: The text describes this as the pattern at smaller token windows.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared activation patching at refusal-onset and final-token regions with a wider token window.
rows.baseline: Refusal-onset intervention compared with final-token intervention
rows.value: The final-token window slightly surpasses the refusal-onset window.
rows.note: The authors attribute this to the wider final-token window overlapping upstream refusal-onset activations.
rows.check: 'Reversed' here is relative to the onset-dominance pattern, not a claim version. The authors attribute it to window overlap.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared activation patching at refusal-onset and final-token regions.
rows.baseline: Final-token intervention compared with refusal-onset intervention
rows.value: The refusal-onset intervention has greater causal efficacy in intermediate layers than the final-token intervention; numerical values are figure only.
rows.note: The text describes the pattern as similar to Qwen2.5.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Patched malicious-run hidden states into benign runs with a 3-layer sliding window across three harmful-content examples.

conditions.value: cyberattack, adult content, and illegal activity examples

rows.measure: Refusal Loss and successful refusal induction
rows.value: The text reports semantic anchors and subsequent tokens as localized causal regions; numerical values are figure only.
rows.note: The reported result concerns localized activation patching, not a single direction.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Projected ROI-level representations onto the unsafe-minus-benign class-contrast direction using the RePE-Mean readout, then classified prompts.
rows.note: Detection separability result; it does not measure refusal behavior.
rows.check: Rows R9–R28 are baselines compared with the study's own detector (Tables 5–6). They are detection scores at an XSTest-calibrated threshold, not refusal behaviour. They are kept as related findings only. The direction is an unsafe-minus-benign class contrast over the ROI on PKU-SafeRLHF/Toxic-Chat data, not the original recipe.
